item.title: Flex Your Emotional Intelligence at Work
item.description:
Career

Flex Your Emotional Intelligence at Work

Accurate workplace use of psychology terms can show your emotional intelligence.

Posted November 8, 2026

Key points
  • Flex your emotional intelligence at work to solidify your professionalism.
  • Correctly use psychology terms and concepts to identify the dysfunctional dynamic beneath the surface.
  • This frees you from getting dragged into drama, having to pick a side, and from bad-mouthing people.

Therapy lingo has become a “thing” on social media, and it is helpful when it illuminates important psychological concepts like “gaslighting” or “trauma bonding.” It can be especially useful in a professional setting when being perceived as emotionally intelligent is important. Possibly the best by-product, however, is that it can prevent you from getting dragged into drama, aggressively taking a side, or bashing anyone. Essentially, by identifying the psychological dynamic beneath the surface, you are providing empathy and wisdom in a constructive and professional manner. Before you try it, however, you may want to do your research to ensure that you are using the terms correctly. Six examples may help clarify how it sounds.

Example 1: Recognizing Triangulation in Workplace Conflicts

Your teammate asks you to lunch because he needs help dealing with a colleague. He explains, “I told him that I was drawing a line and that I would not finish the project for him this time... The next thing I know, he is talking to everyone about me behind my back. He, literally, turned my closest co-worker against me. Now, they are work 'besties,' and neither of them will talk to me."

Response: That hurts, and it is so disappointing. It sounds like triangulation, which is very manipulative. I may have a book that can help.

You highlight that when the co-worker does not get what he wants from a person, he can be passive aggressive, aligning other people with him and against them, which is called “triangulation.”

Example 2: Addressing Victim Stance and Demand for Accountability

Your work friend stops by your office because she is angry and needs to vent. She laments, “I cannot stand being on projects with Dave. I know he has had a hard life, but why do I have to suffer because of it? Every time there is work to do, he complains that he doesn’t feel good, or that the boss is being mean to him, or that his car broke down, or that he just got scammed, or that he is being evicted…. He gets out of doing any work every time! It is infuriating."

Response: It sounds like he uses a victim stance. That is so frustrating. I read somewhere that it is important to calmly and respectfully hold people accountable—no matter what.

You empathize with your friend, but also highlight the possibility of a cognitive distortion (victim stance) that may need to be confronted.

Example 3: Understanding Projection and Envy in the Workplace

Your friend from another department calls and says, “I am so panicked when I am in meetings with Maureen. I work my tail off and do a fantastic job, which is backed by my client’s feedback and my stats, but she calls me 'lazy' and 'apathetic' in front of everyone."

Response: That is so humiliating, and those sound like mischaracterizations. You are none of those things. She may be threatened by your competence and is struggling to handle her jealousy in a healthy manner.

By reassuring her that you believe she is being misperceived, you are supporting her while alerting her to the possibility that the colleague may not be managing her envy in a mature way. When her colleague name-calls, she may be “projecting.”

Example 4: Identifying Codependency and Setting Healthy Boundaries

You ask your co-worker to grab lunch, but she says she can’t because of her suitemate. She says, “Chad needs a lot of help. I feel sorry for him. I help him with all of his projects, and I finish his quotes because he is not good with numbers, but he still throws a fit about his workload, so I end up working through lunch every day just to try and help."

Response: You feel for Chad, which makes you a good person in my opinion, but it sounds like it has become codependent. My therapist usually advises me to detach and get perspective with certain people. By taking a step back, I can figure out whether I am enabling the person.

This example uses multiple psychosocial terms: codependent, detachment, and enabling, to illuminate the problematic nature of the relationship, and the need for an intervention.

Example 5: Navigating Anxious Attachment Styles in Colleagues

A colleague comes to your office and says, “I really like working with Lisa, but she is so clingy. She cannot do anything without me. I tried to go for walks on my breaks last week and she insisted on coming with me every time. I cannot even go to the bathroom without her following me."

Response: That’s frustrating. She may have an anxious attachment style. I know how aggravating it can be. Even though it’s difficult, I try to calmly and kindly set boundaries in those situations.

You are identifying the root of the problem is the person’s attachment style, which may not change, so the person may need to implement limits in the relationship.

Example 6: Recognizing Insight and Self-Awareness Deficits

A co-worker approaches you and confides, "Ann continually and incessantly criticizes me for things, but she turns around and does the exact same thing. I cannot take it. She is such a hypocrite."

Response: That is so irritating. It sounds like she may have deficits with insight and self-awareness.

In this example, you empathize, but also suggest that there may be a flaw in Ann's emotional maturity, that may prevent her from embodying emotionally intelligent tendencies.

Work relationships can be difficult and continually getting dragged into the middle of drama can be time-consuming and anxiety-inducing. However, the last thing you want is to come off as aloof, detached, and unsupportive of others. You strive to be a safe person to talk to. By attempting to identify the dysfunctional dynamic in a problematic situation, you avoid attacking and bad-mouthing colleagues, which helps you maintain a high level of professionalism. You can find even more information on this topic in my book, How to Outsmart a Narcissist, Use Emotional Intelligence to Regain Control at Home, at Work, and in Life.

item.title: Coping With an Acute Injury or Health Diagnosis
item.description:
Anxiety

Coping With an Acute Injury or Health Diagnosis

How to manage change and loss and still live your life.

Posted November 8, 2026

Key points
  • An injury or new diagnosis can feel like an emotional roller coaster ride that you never wanted to take.
  • You may be experiencing change and worry about when and if you will return to your “normal” self.
  • Uncertainty does not automatically mean bad. The worst-case scenario may never come to pass.
Source: Sandjaya/Pixabay

Many clients who come to see me in therapy are coping with an acute injury or health change. For example, they may have sustained an injury while playing a sport or been given a new medical diagnosis. A sudden injury or health change can feel shocking and is often difficult to cope with. You may be trying to adjust to changes in mobility and functioning and worried about when and if you will return to your “normal” self.

Often, the most pressing concern is: Will I get better? And when? The uncertainty is difficult to tolerate. While some injuries or diagnoses have clear treatment plans and timelines, more often it is not crystal clear what someone’s recovery or medical journey will look like. The anxious brain likes to jump to worst-case scenarios when uncertainty exists. It takes a “better safe than sorry” approach, leading us to think about all the possible horrible outcomes so we can be prepared. However, these worst-case scenarios may never come to pass, and anxiety can start to take up more and more space in your daily life.

An injury or new diagnosis can feel like a never-ending emotional roller coaster ride that you never wanted to take. It can be challenging to acknowledge the reality of the injury or diagnosis, including sudden changes you may be facing, without thinking that your life is doomed. Below are some strategies for coping with an acute injury or health diagnosis.

Gather information about your injury or diagnosis

It is helpful to be informed about your condition, as a general understanding can help you have effective conversations with health care providers. It is useful to use reputable sources for gathering information, and your medical team may be able to offer resources. Keep in mind that not all of your questions may have firm answers, and there may be limits to what you or your medical team may be able to know.

While it is difficult to tolerate uncertainty, be mindful of not going down an information-gathering rabbit hole that consumes too much of your time and life. If you notice that trying to gather information about your condition is taking over your daily life or that your anxiety is increasing, set time limits for gathering information. For example, 30 to 60 minutes a week.

Express your feelings

A sudden injury or diagnosis can create a wave of emotions. You may feel scared, apprehensive, sad, angry, frustrated, etc. Trying to suppress your emotions can intensify them. Find an authentic way to express how you are feeling. For example, take five to 10 minutes daily to write out your thoughts or feelings, say them aloud on a voice memo app, or share how you are feeling with a trusted friend or family member. If it feels unfamiliar and anxiety-provoking to talk about your feelings, consider doing so in a less focused or pressured environment. For instance, you may talk about your feelings while traveling in the car with soft music playing.

Seek support and accept help from others

It can be unfamiliar and challenging for some people to accept help from others. Maybe you are used to doing everything yourself, and accepting help leads you to feel incapable. However, accepting help from others allows people who care about you to be of assistance during a difficult time. This is beneficial for them as well as for you. Also, spend time with people you are comfortable with and enjoy. It is natural to feel down, withdraw from others, and isolate ourselves during stressful periods. Yet, isolation can worsen mood. Even if you don’t initially feel like it, carve out some time with others. Your desire to be with others may increase over time. Also, it may be helpful to seek out connection with others who have the same injury or diagnosis. Talking with others with a shared understanding and hearing about others’ treatments, recovery, and coping strategies can feel relieving and supportive.

Set realistic expectations and goals

It can be difficult to accept limitations or the reality that there are some things you may not be able to do or need to do in a different way. It is important to give yourself space and time to grieve any losses you are experiencing. Expecting too much of yourself or trying to ignore the current circumstances can lead to increased frustration, anger, and sadness. Also, trying to meet unrealistic goals may deplete you and lead to less functioning and ability than you would have if you set more realistic and sustainable goals.

Just because you have limitations or there are certain things you cannot do does not mean you are incapable. Non-judgmentally ask yourself what you can and want to realistically take on, and aim to set small, doable goals.

Focus on what brings you meaning and purpose

A new injury or diagnosis can be anxiety-provoking and scary, and can highlight what or who you care most about. Certain activities may be different now, yet there are likely things or people who continue to be meaningful to you. Carve out time for them. Stay connected, or reconnect, to what feels most important and fulfilling to you. You may find that many of these things are simple and joyful, such as spending time with loved ones or time in nature.

Remember that uncertainty does not automatically mean bad

The anxious part of our minds equates uncertainty with bad based on self-protection and preservation. While a good outcome is not guaranteed, neither is a bad one. The future could be incredibly difficult, and it also could be better than you are thinking or neutral. When your mind wants to leap ahead to worst-case scenarios, pause, take a slow breath, and remind yourself, “Uncertain does not mean bad; it simply means unknown.” Then refocus on the present moment and a values-based action you can take today.

item.title: Veterans Day, Service, Music, and Gratitude
item.description:
Gratitude

Veterans Day, Service, Music, and Gratitude

Let music guide you to deeper respect and gratitude for those who served.

Posted November 8, 2026

Key points
  • Veterans Day music reminds us that behind every ceremony is a person and a story.
  • Music slows us down to feel the true weight of gratitude beyond a simple greeting.
  • Let veteran soundtracks remind us that gratitude is listening, not just thanking.

“Thank you for your service.” At a checkout counter, at an airport, or in a hallway, there’s rarely time to say much more. We offer our thanks and continue with the day.

At a Veterans Day ceremony, music could give us a little longer to consider what we’re thanking someone for.

When a bugler plays “Taps,” people grow quiet. Some bow their heads; others look toward the flag or watch the musician. Someone remembering a friend’s funeral may find those notes difficult to hear. A child attending a ceremony for the first time may look to a parent to understand why everyone has stopped talking. We hear the same music, but it brings different memories to each of us.

The Power of the National Anthem to Unite and Reflect

The national anthem gathers us in another way. Some people sing confidently; others search for a comfortable octave or stand silently. For a few minutes, we give our attention to something we share. What we make of that moment varies, especially in a country where our disagreements run deep. Still, it can be moving to hear people make the effort to sing together. And we may respectfully wonder about those who don’t stand.

Ceremonies have their place. We come together to honor, to remember, and to share those who have served and what we have in common as Americans. We also want to know more about the people we have gathered to honor.

People leave military service with very different feelings about their time in uniform. Some speak readily about it. Others have little interest in revisiting those years, particularly with someone they barely know. Pride may sit alongside grief or disappointment. Friendships can endure for a lifetime, as can questions about what happened and why.

The Conversational Power of Music Among Veterans

A song may open a conversation. Maybe it was the one everyone complained about in the barracks, then sang along anyway. Someone else might remember listening through headphones during a long wait, or hearing a recording sent from home. A ridiculous song might bring back a friend more vividly than a formal tribute. A love song might bring back the person waiting at home.

Playing a medley of the armed forces songs is interesting, inspiring, and even surprising. When we listened to the medley, we were surprised to know the words or at least remember the tune to every song. They stir deeply, each bringing back a memory, an image. They do remind us to honor the service of individuals and the corps of fellow citizens who helped ensure and sustain our democracy.

We know how a few bars of music can take us somewhere: to the kitchen of a childhood home, a college roommate, a drive we had almost forgotten. For a veteran, a song from those years may be welcome, painful, or both.

“What did you listen to then?” gives someone room to decide where to begin and how much to share. The answer may have little to do with combat or sacrifice. It may be about being nineteen, missing home, or discovering a musician whose recordings became a lifelong companion.

We would like to hear more of those stories in the ways we observe Veterans Day. A school could invite a veteran to choose a piece of music and talk about its place in their life. A community concert could include songs local veterans suggest, along with the memories they choose to share. At home, a family might listen to a recording together and discover something they had never thought to ask.

How to Respond When Veterans Share Their Stories

We may hear an account that unsettles our assumptions about service. Someone may prefer to talk about the music itself. If they do, we can follow their lead.

Veterans Day also gives the rest of us reason to examine our responsibilities. Freedom, equality, the rule of law, and human dignity depend on what people do in ordinary civic life. Honoring service includes caring for veterans and their families, and considering how faithfully we uphold the ideals we invoke at ceremonies.

This Veterans Day reminds us that we are seeking a more perfect union and that we are one people. With gratitude.

Ed Browder, Viet Nam, who lives with pride.
Source: Mort Sherman

This November, I hope we make time for the familiar tributes and for a few personal songs. After the ceremony, someone beside us may have a story about a recording they’ve kept for fifty years, or a friend who always sang off-key.

The tunes of America reverberate deeply.

item.title: Are You Waiting for Life to Begin?
item.description:
Personal Perspectives

Are You Waiting for Life to Begin?

Personal Perspective: Do you miss the version of yourself who felt alive?

Posted November 8, 2026

Key points
  • What we miss most is not the person themselves, but the version of ourselves we became in their presence.
  • Waiting for the right person, opportunity can turn the life we are living into something we postpone.
  • Even when life does not unfold as we imagined, we can learn to notice moments of joy in the life we have now.
  • A meaningful connection can change us, but we do not have to remain attached to that person to preserve it.

What if the person who brings you to life is also the one who brings you pain?

I was thinking about my own life and how, sometimes, it can feel as though it is divided into two halves: the life we live and the life we imagine sharing with a particular person.

When I tried to picture it, I saw a page divided by a crooked line (like the line in a broken-heart emoji). Another line runs alongside it, following its shape, inseparable from it. It was the connection, even when the two people were no longer together.

Connection
Source: Aigerim Alpysbekova

If you look at this picture, you might see different things. But I see three beings. Two who could not be more different, yet somehow belong to each other. And a third one: The space between them. The grey that separates their worlds, yet also connects them. That line is a boundary and a bridge.

Sometimes, light passes through that grey and reaches the other side, turning it bright for a moment. Life becomes colorful again. There is love, warmth, and a feeling that the world might be beautiful. But when the light fades, they return to their separate worlds, to the lives they have to live apart.

Maybe it is that space between the two moments, the third part of the picture, where you find yourself suspended in midair, unable to move forward or backward, not knowing where you stand.

One becomes the freedom. The other becomes the weight that gives that freedom meaning. But perhaps neither is as free as they seem. One does not know how to stop giving. The other does not know how to stop holding on. That is why some connections are so difficult to explain: they bring out parts of us we rarely see, beautiful, yet painful.

The life we spend waiting for

But what if the grey world in this picture is not only about the space between two people? What if it is also about the way we live?

Think about how much of our lives we spend waiting. Waiting for the right person, the right opportunity, the right moment. We look at our present lives and see only the grey. We imagine that once someone arrives, once we finally get what we have been longing for, we will begin to live.

But while we wait for that moment, what happens to the life we are already living?

We begin to believe that life is waiting for us somewhere in the future, beyond that line. This is why some connections are so powerful. For a moment, they remind us that we can feel something we thought we had lost. Something so human that, for a second, the rest of the world vanishes. We think we miss the person, but we miss the version of ourselves who felt that alive in their presence.

Have you ever considered that the person who awakened something inside you might not be the only place where that part of you can exist? What if the freedom, the love were yours all along, even before you met them? Maybe they helped you discover a part of yourself you never knew existed.

The connection was real. What you felt was real. It could have been painful, beautiful, and unlike anything you had experienced before. None of that becomes less meaningful just because the connection ended. But why do we have to hold on to the person to keep what they helped us discover?

Maybe it is possible to let someone go without having to erase what happened. Keep the part of yourself that came alive. You do not have to return to the connection to feel those things again. You can carry them into the rest of your life.

What I would tell my younger self

I know that looking inside yourself isn't comfortable. It means accepting some things, questioning others, and making sense of your own feelings. It also means recognizing that a new person is not responsible for the pain left by someone who came before them.

I would tell my younger self that it is okay not to have everything figured out. It is okay to take your time. And it is okay to miss someone without going back to them.

And if you are living in the grey right now, remember that the part of you that can see the light is still there. You may have stopped looking for it. Sometimes, all you need is to believe that the other side exists. But life on the grey side can be beautiful, too, if you allow yourself to see it. An ordinary morning can be warmth, joy in a small moment, and beauty in places you might have overlooked. And when you finally see it, let yourself feel it fully.

You might ask, what is the point of all this? Well, first of all, thank you for reading almost to the end. But if I had to leave you with just one thought, it's this: no matter where you are, whom you are with, or what circumstances you are living through, your life is still yours. You may not always have a choice about what happens, but you have some choice in how you meet it. You can spend your days holding on to what hurts, waiting for life to be different, or you can slowly begin noticing the beautiful things that are already here.

There is life everywhere, even in the dirt. And no, that doesn't mean we have to pretend everything is fine or feel grateful for every difficult thing that happens. It means that even in an imperfect life, there is still something worth noticing.

Your light is always there, with you. You do not have to spend your life waiting for someone else to turn it on.

item.title: When the World Doesn't Say Thank You
item.description:
Loneliness

When the World Doesn't Say Thank You

On loneliness, belonging, and learning self-regard.

Posted November 8, 2026

Key points
  • Loneliness can leave us feeling invisible, even to ourselves.
  • We often look to others for reassurance that we matter.
  • Others' silence isn't a measure of our worth.
Source: Pete Pedroza/Unsplash

For a while, one of the most reliable relationships in my life was with a traffic sign.

It was one of those electronic billboards you see on the outskirts of villages that nags you for how fast you're driving. Go too fast and the numbers flash red. Keep to the speed limit and you're rewarded with two words of appreciation:

THANK YOU.

I became a bit too fond of that sign. Embarrassingly, some days I would deliberately crawl past it, making sure I was going at exactly the right speed, just to receive its validation. And it delivered. Every time.

“You're most welcome,” I'd think, feeling absurdly pleased with myself.

Now, you might reasonably wonder why a mature woman would get quite so much satisfaction from being thanked by an illuminated slab of roadside equipment.

It was a particularly lonely period.

I'd recently returned from Switzerland, and was trying to find my feet in a community where I'd once felt very much at home. Much had changed in my absence, and cultivating a sense of belonging was proving difficult.

I was living alone, feeling bereft, and some days the only living creature I spoke to was an elderly cat. Not to be too judgy, but although he was selectively affectionate, his vocabulary wasn’t up to much. So the traffic sign became an accidental but welcome addition to my social circle.

I knew perfectly well that it was only thanking me for driving at the appropriate speed, but I looked forward to those two little words dropping into my day. It felt good to be acknowledged and, truthfully, I wanted some reassurance that I hadn't disappeared.

How Loneliness Changes Our Need for Validation

I've been reflecting on that period recently, and about how much we rely on other people to remind us who we are. It's a backdrop we barely notice when life is flowing along reasonably well. We have our familiar routines, people to talk to, and places to go. There's a sense of belonging that we probably take for granted until our circumstances change.

I think this is one of the reasons loneliness can be so unsettling. Alongside the sadness of having nobody to share things with, there's the strange experience of chalking up an entire day without anyone witnessing it.

You might have achieved something substantial, or white-knuckled your way through a thoroughly miserable morning. Maybe you made a particularly earthy soup with the leeks from your garden, and nobody noticed.

One unremarkable Tuesday, I remember calculating how long it would take my neighbors to realise I hadn’t collected the milk from my doorstep. Three days, I wagered.

The Gap Between Understanding and Practicing Self-Worth

Having written a book called Change Your Words, Change Your World, I've spent much of my working life exploring how language affects the way we feel about ourselves, so I’m quite familiar with the idea of self-worth. In theory, at least. In practice, knowing something intellectually doesn't necessarily mean you're proficient at applying it when life gets difficult.

Like you, no doubt, I've caught myself looking for digital reassurance. A message from someone I care about can lift my spirits enormously. Equally, the absence of a reply can fill my head with squirrels and I’ll waste a couple of hours wondering what I've done wrong.

Wanting to feel appreciated is human. The trouble is that other people are unreliable sources of reassurance because they have their own lives to get on with. Sometimes they’re just busy running a taxi service for their kids and don’t get your message until bedtime. Other times they’re having enthralling conversations with their own cats.

Meanwhile, we're wondering whether we've somehow offended the entire human race. It's exhausting. And I wonder how much of that exhaustion comes from constantly looking outside ourselves for something we might be able to offer ourselves.

We’re often much kinder to other people. If a friend tells us she's had a dreadful day, we don't usually ask her to produce evidence; we listen, sympathise, maybe make her a cup of tea. However, when it comes to our own shortcomings, we can be surprisingly dismissive.

What Is Self-Compassion and How Can We Practice It?

Psychologist Kristin Neff has spent years researching self-compassion, including how we can learn to respond to our own challenges with the understanding we'd offer a friend.

It sounds perfectly sensible, doesn't it? But when you’re feeling lonely or discouraged, do you comfort yourself, or spend time forensically investigating what you’ve done to end up that way?

This year I’ve decided to take a different approach. Whenever that familiar feeling of being disappointed or overlooked colors my perspective, I pause and acknowledge what's actually happening.

Is it possible I was hoping someone would call, or do I just need a hug? There's often a little relief in admitting that, even if nothing changes immediately.

It doesn't always work, of course. Some days I'd like the universe to send me a personalised letter of appreciation, preferably on headed paper.

I wonder what I’d say now to the woman who used to drive past that traffic sign. I'd tell her I understood why she was lonely, and that it was perfectly reasonable to miss the life she'd had, even though she might not believe me.

Perhaps that's the thing about learning to validate ourselves. It's easy enough to understand the idea, but quite another matter to feel it. I don't think I've entirely worked it out yet, but I’m getting better at noticing when I’m waiting for someone else to tell me I’m doing all right.

It still feels a little unnatural, but then so did developing an emotional attachment to a traffic sign. I still smile whenever I drive past one and receive my THANK YOU. And I always make sure I'm going at the right speed. It would be a shame to disappoint an old friend.

item.title: Don't Let Future You Lead Present You Astray
item.description:
Motivation

Don't Let Future You Lead Present You Astray

Research shows that we identify more with our future self than our past self.

Posted November 8, 2026

Key points
  • The decisions that we make involve consulting both our past and future "self."
  • New research shows that we identify more with our future self than with our past self.
  • This identification is based on the belief that we will change less in the future than we have in the past.
This Way.
Source: Susan O Yin/Unsplash

I have a friend who pays $99.99 a month for an unlimited gym membership he never uses. When his annual renewal came up back in October, I asked him if he was going to finally let it drop and give himself a $1,200 raise, and his reply was as predictable as it was perplexing. “Are you kidding?” he said. “Cold weather is right around the corner.” Refraining from pointing out that he didn’t darken the door of the gym during the short cold days of last winter, I let the matter drop.

Truth be told, as irrational (not to mention expensive) as my friend’s fruitless gym membership is, his seemingly capricious behavior is by no means unique to him. Most of us occasionally make plans for our future that our behavior in the past would suggest we ought to reconsider. The easy explanation for such poor planning is that it’s easier to make plans than to follow through with them, but a series of studies recently published in Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin suggests that there may be an even more interesting explanation for the behavior. According to the studies, we often ignore our past track record when making future plans because we identify less with our “self” in the past that we have already lived than we do with our self in the future that has not yet arrived.

In a total of 12 online studies conducted in nine different countries including the U.S., participants were asked to rate the level of connectedness of their current self with their past self, and their equidistant future self. Randomly assigned to one of three conditions—future-to-current, current-to-future, and current-to-past—participants were presented with seven pairs of circles that ranged from barely touching to almost completely overlapping. They were then asked to select the pair of circles that most accurately represented how “similar and connected” their current self was to their self of several years in the past (five years in some of the studies, 10 in others), or to their self of the same number of years in the future (depending on which condition they were assigned to).

People Identify More With Their Future Self Than Past Self

Across all of the studies, participants perceived their current self to be more similar to their future self than to their past self. Regardless of the time period separating the current self from the past or future self (five years or 10), or whether they were thinking forward from their current to future self, or looking backward from their future to their current self, it was the future self with which participants felt more of a connection. The finding also held true across age groups and cultural contexts, as represented by the nine different countries involved in the studies.

The sense of connection with our future self, the researchers found, stems from an underestimation of how much we will change in the future relative to how much we have changed in the past. Because our future selves are more abstract than our past selves, being based on imagined rather than remembered details, we have a hard time imagining the sort of changes we have undergone in the past also occurring in our future. And this belief that our future self is more stable than our past self leads us to identify more closely with, and feel a stronger emotional connection to, our future self than to our past self.

Interestingly, the researchers found that this sense of connection with our future self extends to the goals and preferences that guide our decision-making. The things that we view as important right now, we believe, will remain similarly important to us in the future, regardless of how much such priorities might have changed for us in the past. And since the decisions we make for our future are based on how satisfied we believe they will make us, this overestimation of how stable our goals are can lead us to disregard our concrete past experience in favor of an abstract sense of future satisfaction. In other words, a weaker sense of connection with our past self, as compared with our future self, can limit our ability to learn from past experience.

Consequences of Prioritizing Future Self Over Past Experience

As abstract as the concept of a “future self” may seem, our tendency to identify with it at the expense of our past self could potentially have some very concrete consequences by causing us to “apply different evaluative criteria for decisions made by different selves across time.” Contemplating a career change, for example, or speculating on a risky but lucrative financial investment—or, on a lesser note, considering whether or not to renew a gym membership we never use-- we can easily overestimate our future satisfaction with a given decision because we don’t give sufficient weight to our dissatisfaction with similar decisions we have made in the past.

It’s certainly useful to consult our imaginary future selves in such decisions, but we would be well-advised to also pay serious heed to the advice of our more experienced past selves. We might not like what they have to tell us, but we disregard the advice at our own expense.

item.title: The Inner Voice Isn't Always the Inner Enemy
item.description:
Personal Perspectives

It's Not You, It's Who You Represent

The inner voice isn't always your inner enemy.

Posted November 8, 2026

Key points
  • Imposter syndrome is a psychological experience where you persistently doubt your abilities.
  • Pausing is your superpower.
  • The voice of the unreliable narrator in your head is not your own.

For a long time, I felt like an imposter. Although I had graduated from medical school, passed the internal medicine boards, and completed a residency, part of me still grappled with imposter syndrome.

Imposter syndrome (also called the impostor phenomenon) is when you persistently doubt your abilities, feel like a fraud, and fear others will expose you, even when you have clear proof of your success.

I suppose it had to do with my early childhood. I was molested from the ages of 11 to 13. I told my parents, but when they confronted the senior Boy Scout leaders, they were shamed into silence. I was left with an undying feeling that it was all my fault. I internalized this, and that gave birth to a voice inside my head that wasn’t my own. It belonged to my perpetrator, who installed it in me when I didn’t have the language to refute it.

Alcohol as a coping mechanism

While I engaged with several therapists over decades, I foolishly believed that the shame I was attempting to overcome was something I could outrun, suppress, or avoid. And for a while, I believed I had. The proof was clear: I became a married physician. I was successful, and yet when the COVID-19 pandemic hit, all the pillars that had quietly moored me to my external life disappeared. In that isolation, shame came roaring back.

I, like millions of Americans, ran to alcohol to cope.

The unreliable narrator took hold

Throughout this period, the voice inside my head, the one I dubbed the unreliable narrator, played on an endless loop. He told me that I was too much, or not enough, or fundamentally broken. I believed him because, well, he was the voice in my head. I was ill-equipped to challenge this voice or ask whether these were facts or simply thoughts. It never occurred to me because that voice lived so clearly inside me that challenging him meant challenging the very framework that had made me a success.

This conflict became apparent when my beloved manager, an Ivy League professor, called me idiotic. No, he didn’t call me an idiot, though he might as well have. He said "idiotic," and I internalized that word and shut down. I couldn’t speak. I couldn't breathe. It was a truly embarrassing experience.

Eventually, I recovered, but I sat with that moment for a long time. What I came to understand much later was that, by using the term idiotic, my beloved manager activated an old trauma I had locked away in my subconscious. My former child molester often called me an idiot. When my manager used that word in a conversation with my adult self, it triggered a trauma response in my younger self—fight, flight, or freeze. My body chose freeze.

The power of the pause

What I learned from this experience is the power of the pause—pausing is your superpower. Far too many of us respond quickly, often talking before the other person has finished their sentence. But I took it a step further and developed the four P’s: pause, present, ponder, and possibilities.

The trick is you have to practice when you’re not activated. Next time you’re speaking to your friend, when they stop talking, don’t answer. Pause. Count to three, check in with yourself, be present, ponder the situation, and then, and only then, can you see the possibilities.

Let’s revisit that scenario with my manager

He uses the word idiotic.

Pause. Count to three.

Stay present.

Internal self: “What’s going on with you now?”

Activated self: “I'm feeling my face flush. My heart is racing.”

Ponder.

Internal self: “Okay, you’re experiencing shame. Do you have any idea why?"

Activated self: “My child molester used to call me an idiot.”

Internal self: “Okay, but you’re not an idiot. In fact, you’re not 11 years old. You’re an adult doctor, and this situation has nothing to do with what happened to you decades ago."

Possibilities

Internal self: “Now that you understand your manager activated some old trauma, how would you like to respond?"

Activated self: “You asked a good question. It deserves some thought. Let me get back to you.”

Remember: You can't think your way out of shame that lives in your nervous system.

Shame is a well-intentioned guard dog with terrible judgment about what constitutes actual danger.
